title: How to Leverage Domain Expertise — Chris Lovejoy, Notius Labs

primary.label: AI Product, UX & Human Factors

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's core focus is how domain experts supervise, correct, and collaborate with AI products through three human-in-the-loop organizational models (Oracle, Evaluator, Architect). The framework is cross-vertical with healthcare case studies (Tandem, Anterior) and a personal-productivity case study (Granola meeting notes). Covers building AI products from initial Oracle model through scaling to automated Architect systems, spanning development, growth, and continuous improvement. Assumes basic familiarity with AI product development and vertical SaaS but requires no deep technical or engineering background. Conference presentation at AI Engineer featuring a framework with three case studies and audience Q&A. All cited evidence is directly stated in the transcript with grade said_in_transcript.

summary: Chris Lovejoy, a former medical doctor turned AI builder, presents a framework for leveraging domain expertise in AI products through three organizational models: the Oracle, the Evaluator, and the Architect. He argues that winning in vertical AI is fundamentally an organizational problem rather than a model-quality problem, citing Gartner data that ~50% of generative AI projects were abandoned last year. Three case studies make the framework tangible. Granola, an AI meeting notes company valued over $1B, uses the Oracle model: a writer and journalist hired as first employee wrote all prompts, conducted extensive user research, and continues as primary gatekeeper of AI quality—assessing outputs and making improvements directly. Tandem, a medical AI scribe, started with a single doctor as Oracle but evolved into a decentralized Oracle with multiple doctors covering different specialties, countries, and note types. Anterior, a prior authorization startup, progressed through all three models—Oracle to Evaluator to Architect—as scale and variation in policy interpretation demanded automated, self-improving systems. Lovejoy details skills for each role: the Oracle needs direct use-case experience plus prompting and attention to detail; the Evaluator needs domain expertise plus data science intuition, statistical skills, leadership, and product management; the Architect needs domain expertise, LLM product experience, and engineering skills. He then outlines three principles for leveraging domain experts. First, define a principal domain expert: a single individual accountable for AI quality, avoiding consensus-by-committee. Second, give them genuine ownership rather than treating them as consultants—Lovejoy shares a failure case where two senior clinicians lacked clear ownership, progress was slow, and both left within 12–18 months. Third, hire for breadth: domain expertise is the base requirement, but hire someone with as many adjacent skills as possible so they can grow from Oracle to Evaluator to Architect; gaps can be filled by pairing with specialists. He closes by noting the playbook is still being figured out as the industry is early in building AI-powered products with domain expertise.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Winning in vertical AI is fundamentally an organizational problem, not a model quality problem—front-end models are good enough, the gap is operationalizing expert judgment

Three organizational models: Oracle (expert does both assessment and improvement), Evaluator (expert defines and measures quality, engineers improve), Architect (expert designs self-improving systems)
Organizations typically start with the Oracle model and evolve based on scale pressure, metric availability, and automation feasibility—as seen in Granola, Tandem, and Anterior
For the Oracle role, hire for direct experience of the specific use case, not just a credential; prompting and content engineering are learnable

Hiring someone who is only a domain expert creates a growth ceiling; they cannot evolve from Oracle to Evaluator to Architect, forcing the organization to bring in new people

sections.title: Introduction and Speaker Background
sections.summary: Chris Lovejoy introduces himself as a former medical doctor (Cambridge-trained, NHS) who moved into AI in 2018, working at Tandem, Anterior (as first employee), and other startups. His recurring challenge was building products that bake in domain expertise to create differentiated AI. He references his previous AI Engineer conference talk on the last mile problem, viewed by ~100,000 people, which prompted the question of how to structure organizations to leverage domain expertise.

sections.title: Why Vertical AI Matters and Common Mistakes
sections.summary: Lovejoy frames vertical AI as a major opportunity—vertical SaaS was ~$50B while AI in the labor force is multi-trillion—but notes ~50% of generative AI projects were abandoned (Gartner), often because products lack deep understanding of the workflows they automate. He identifies three common mistakes: not hiring domain experts or hiring too late, hiring the wrong type, and not fitting them into the organization appropriately.

sections.title: The Oracle-Evaluator-Architect Framework
sections.summary: Lovejoy introduces three models for incorporating domain expertise. The Oracle directly embeds expertise into the application, performing both assessment and improvement. The Evaluator defines what quality means and sets up measurement systems, then works with engineers who implement improvements. The Architect designs self-improving systems that learn from user interactions with minimal human-in-the-loop.

sections.title: Decision Guide and Organizational Evolution
sections.summary: Lovejoy provides a decision guide: if performance cannot be objectively measured and taste matters more, use the Oracle. If metrics exist and manual iteration is fast enough, the Evaluator suffices. If iteration is too slow and automation methods are identifiable, progress to Architect. Organizations often start as Oracle and evolve when things break at scale.

sections.title: Case Study: Granola—Oracle at Scale
sections.summary: Granola, an AI meeting notes company valued over $1B, exemplifies the Oracle model. Joe, a writer and journalist hired as first employee, wrote all prompts, conducted extensive user research (reading papers, talking to thousands of users), and serves as primary gatekeeper of AI quality—assessing outputs and making improvements directly. This works because there is no objectively perfect meeting note, taste is central, and the core output is amenable to direct human review even at scale. They also run evals and have internal tooling, but fundamentally operate as an Oracle.

sections.title: Case Study: Tandem—Decentralized Oracle
sections.summary: Tandem's medical AI scribe started with Roy, a doctor with McKinsey experience, as a single Oracle reviewing medical notes and updating prompts. As scale made this impossible for one person, they evolved to a decentralized Oracle, hiring doctors across different specialties, countries, and note types. The platform supports a long tail of thousands or more prompt customizations, with each domain expert owning a particular subset or customer relationship. This works because medical expertise is required, subjectivity exists, and variation demands many specialized experts.

sections.title: Case Study: Anterior—Oracle to Evaluator to Architect
sections.summary: Anterior's prior authorization product progressed through all three models. Lovejoy as first technical employee started as Oracle (building prompts/code, clinically reviewing outputs). As customers and variation grew, he evolved to Evaluator—defining metrics and failure modes, building a review dashboard, hiring clinicians to perform reviews, and collaborating with engineers. When manual iteration by engineers could not handle variation in how organizations interpret policies, he moved to Architect, designing automated improvement systems that learn from usage. AI quality here is clearly measurable: outputs are either correct or incorrect based on medical evidence.

sections.title: Skills Needed for Each Role
sections.summary: Lovejoy details skills for each model. The Oracle needs relevant domain expertise—specifically direct experience of the use case (not just a credential)—plus prompting, attention to detail, and customer communication. The Evaluator needs domain expertise plus data science intuition (defining metrics, building measurement systems), statistical skills, industry connections for hiring, leadership, and product management experience. The Architect needs domain expertise, experience with LLM-powered products (knowing levers for improvement), and engineering skills.

sections.title: Principles for Leveraging Domain Experts
sections.summary: Lovejoy begins outlining three principles for leveraging domain experts. First, define a principal domain expert: a single individual accountable for AI quality who can make decisions, avoiding consensus-by-committee where nobody is truly responsible. Second, give them genuine ownership rather than treating them as consultants—have them in the room when decisions are made to build a differentiated product. A third principle is introduced but not completed in this section.

sections.title: Principle Three—Hiring for Breadth and Failure Modes
sections.summary: Lovejoy elaborates on the importance of building a system around the principal expert for accurate measurement and improvement. He shares a failure case: one company had two co-equal senior clinicians with no clear principal, limited ownership, and an advisory role—resulting in slow progress on AI quality systems, and both leaving within 12–18 months, taking institutional context with them. He then presents the third principle: hire for breadth. Domain expertise is the base requirement, but candidates should have as many adjacent skills as possible (e.g., statistics, data science, engineering). Gaps can be filled by pairing with specialists. The failure mode is hiring someone who is only a domain expert, creating a growth ceiling that prevents evolution from Oracle to Evaluator to Architect and forcing the organization to bring in new people. Someone who has served as Oracle gains deep insight into AI performance and failure modes, positioning them well to become an Evaluator.

sections.title: Summary and Conclusion
sections.summary: Lovejoy summarizes the talk: assessing AI quality requires domain expertise; three organizational models exist (Oracle, Evaluator, Architect) and the appropriate approach depends on use case and current scale; each requires different adjacent skills. His core advice is to hire a principal domain expert early with relevant expertise and breadth of adjacent skills, give them ownership, start them as an Oracle, and let their role evolve along the appropriate axis as the product and organization grow. He notes the playbook is still being figured out because the industry is early in building AI-powered products with domain expertise. Slides are available on his website; one audience question is taken.
